short: An influential Enlightenment philosopher whose theories of social contract and natural rights heavily shaped modern political thought.
full:
John Locke was a highly influential English philosopher and physician, widely regarded as one of the chief intellectual architects of the Enlightenment. Coming of age during the tumultuous English Civil War, he later became deeply involved in politics through his association with the Earl of Shaftesbury. Locke's most famous philosophical work, *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1689), argued against innate ideas, proposing instead that the human mind is a blank slate (*tabula rasa*) shaped entirely by experience and empirical observation.

His political philosophy proved equally foundational. In his *Two Treatises of Government*, Locke argued against the divine right of kings, proposing that governments derive their legitimacy from the consent of the governed and exist primarily to protect natural rights—life, liberty, and property. If a government fails in this duty, he asserted, citizens have a right to rebel. These ideas provided intellectual justification for the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and later exerted a profound influence on the American Declaration of Independence and the broader development of liberal democracy.
